section.title: The Offerings of the Prince
section.sectionRationale: Having named the prince's duties and boundaries in chapter 45, the vision now shows him in worship: entering, standing, bowing, and providing sacrifices on Sabbaths, New Moons, and feast days, always as a worshiper alongside the people, never as a priest at the altar. The chapter closes with the kitchens where the ordinary sacrifices of the people are cooked, holiness fenced carefully at every point.
section.thesis: Even the prince, the highest human authority in the restored land, worships as a layman under the same ordered access as everyone else, entering and leaving by the same gate as the people and offering through the priests rather than for them, a picture of true leadership that submits to God rather than presuming upon Him.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the shut gate opened for the prince and the people on Sabbaths and New Moons; the fixed and freewill offerings the prince provides across the sacred calendar; a law preserving the people's inheritance from royal confiscation; and the kitchens at the corners of the outer court where the people's sacrifices are cooked.

units.label: The gate opened for worship
units.note: the prince enters as a worshiper among the people

verses.text: “This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘The gate of the inner court that faces east must be kept shut during the six days of work, but on the Sabbath day and on the day of the New Moon it shall be opened.

The {{nasi|prince}} is to enter from the outside through the portico of the gateway and stand by the gatepost, while the priests sacrifice his burnt offerings and peace offerings. He is to bow in worship at the threshold of the gate and then depart, but the gate must not be shut until evening.
On the Sabbaths and New Moons the people of the land are also to bow in worship before the LORD at the entrance to that gateway.
The burnt offering that the prince presents to the LORD on the Sabbath day shall be six unblemished male lambs and an unblemished ram.
The grain offering with the ram shall be one ephah, and the grain offering with the lambs shall be as much as he is able, along with a hin of oil per ephah.
On the day of the New Moon he shall offer a young, unblemished bull, six lambs, and a ram without blemish.
He is to provide a grain offering of an ephah with the bull, an ephah with the ram, and as much as he is able with the lambs, along with a hin of oil per ephah.
When the prince enters, he shall go in through the portico of the gateway, and he shall go out the same way.

units.label: One gate in, the opposite gate out
units.note: the prince among the people, freewill and daily offerings

verses.text: When the people of the land come before the LORD at the appointed feasts, whoever enters by the north gate to worship must go out by the south gate, and whoever enters by the south gate must go out by the north gate. No one is to return through the gate by which he entered, but each must go out by the opposite gate.
When the people enter, the prince shall go in with them, and when they leave, he shall leave.
At the festivals and appointed feasts, the grain offering shall be an ephah with a bull, an ephah with a ram, and as much as one is able to give with the lambs, along with a hin of oil per ephah.

When the prince makes a freewill offering to the LORD, whether a burnt offering or a peace offering, the gate facing east must be opened for him. He is to offer his burnt offering or peace offering just as he does on the Sabbath day. Then he shall go out, and the gate must be closed after he goes out.
And you shall provide an unblemished year-old lamb as a daily burnt offering to the LORD; you are to offer it every morning.

You are also to provide with it every morning a grain offering of a sixth of an ephah with a third of a hin of oil to moisten the fine flour, a grain offering to the LORD. This is a permanent statute.
Thus they shall provide the lamb, the grain offering, and the oil every morning as a regular burnt offering.’

units.label: The prince's inheritance protected
units.note: no confiscation of the people's land

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘If the prince gives a gift to any of his sons as an inheritance, it will belong to his descendants. It will become their property by inheritance.

But if he gives a gift from his inheritance to one of his servants, it will belong to that servant until the year of freedom; then it will revert to the prince. His inheritance belongs only to his sons; it shall be theirs.

The prince must not take any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property. He is to provide an inheritance for his sons from his own property, so that none of My people will be displaced from his property.’”

units.label: The kitchens of the temple
units.note: cooking the people's sacrifices without spreading holiness

verses.text: Then the man brought me through the entrance at the side of the gate into the holy chambers facing north, which belonged to the priests, and he showed me a place there at the far western end

and said to me, “This is the place where the priests shall boil the guilt offering and the {{chatat|sin offering}}, and where they shall bake the grain offering, so that they do not bring them into the outer court and transmit holiness to the people.”
Then he brought me into the outer court and led me around to its four corners, and I saw a separate court in each of its corners.
In the four corners of the outer court there were enclosed courts, each forty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. Each of the four corner areas had the same dimensions.
Around the inside of each of the four courts was a row of masonry with ovens built at the base of the walls on all sides.
And he said to me, “These are the kitchens where those who minister at the temple will cook the {{zebach|sacrifices}} offered by the people.”

nasi.gloss: Prince, chief, one lifted up. In this chapter the nasi is shown worshiping exactly as a layman does, entering and leaving by the same route as the people, never crossing into priestly ministry at the altar itself.

chatat.gloss: Sin offering, purification offering. Even this cooked in a separate, guarded kitchen, so its holiness would not spread carelessly to the ordinary people in the outer court.

zebach.gloss: Sacrifice, a slaughtered offering, often eaten in fellowship. These are the sacrifices brought by the ordinary worshiper, cooked in the corner kitchens rather than in the holy chambers reserved for the priests' portion.

basic.context: Chapter 45 fixed the prince's territory and his duty to supply offerings; chapter 46 shows him actually worshiping. On Sabbaths and New Moons the inner east gate, otherwise shut, opens so the prince may stand at its threshold while the priests sacrifice on his behalf, and the ordinary people bow at the same gate. The prince enters and leaves exactly as he came, never through the gate reserved for the LORD alone in chapter 44, and when the whole community gathers for the feasts, he goes in and out with the people rather than above them. The chapter also protects ordinary Israelites from royal land grabs, echoing the same concern for justice raised in chapter 45, and closes with the practical detail of corner kitchens where the people's own sacrifices are cooked, holiness carefully fenced from spreading where it should not.
basic.hermeneutics: The vision continues to describe rather than legislate; its architectural and ritual precision serves a theological point rather than demanding a literal future replication. The abiding truth is that true leadership, even at its highest earthly level, submits to the same access to God that ordinary worshipers have, and does not presume to stand where only the LORD, or His priests, may stand.
basic.originalLanguages: The nasi, prince, is carefully distinguished throughout from a melek, king; here he worships like anyone else, standing at a threshold rather than at an altar. Even the chatat, sin offering, must be cooked away from the people so its holiness does not spread where it should not, and the zebach, the ordinary worshiper's sacrifice, has its own guarded kitchen in the outer court.
basic.typology: The prince's worship alongside, never above, his people anticipates the true King who, though He alone deserved to stand anywhere, humbled Himself and was numbered among sinners at His baptism and His death. The careful containment of holiness, so it does not leak carelessly into ordinary life, anticipates the moment holiness itself would go out freely to touch and heal rather than merely to be guarded, in the ministry of Jesus.
basic.christ: Philippians 2:6-8 says that though He existed in the form of God, Christ did not consider equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in the likeness of man, He humbled Himself. The prince who enters by the ordinary gate and leaves by the ordinary way, never presuming on the LORD's own entrance, images this same humility: true, divinely appointed authority does not grasp at access it has not been given, a pattern the world's true King fulfilled perfectly, and one He now invites His people to imitate.
basic.god: God cares about the details of ordinary life and worship, not only the grand vision of glory in chapter 43. He fences even the cooking of sacrifices so holiness spreads exactly as intended, and He holds His appointed leader to the same worship pattern as the people he serves, showing that no human office exempts anyone from ordered, humble access to a holy God.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 21:2 and Leviticus 25:10 give the background for the year of freedom mentioned in 46:17, the year when servants and property are released back. 1 Kings 21 tells the story of King Ahab seizing Naboth's inheritance, the very abuse of royal power that 46:18 forbids outright. Philippians 2:6-8 shows the ultimate pattern of humble, non-grasping authority fulfilled in Christ. Ezekiel 44:1-3 sets the earlier restriction on the LORD's own gate that this chapter's prince still respects.
basic.oneStory: Scripture keeps testing whether human rulers will grasp power that is not theirs or serve humbly under God's own reign. Israel's kings so often failed that test, seizing land like Ahab and defiling worship like the kings mourned in chapter 43. Here the coming prince is pictured worshiping humbly among his people, and that picture is fulfilled in Jesus, the true King who did not grasp equality with God but humbled Himself, and who now leads His people not by seizing what is theirs but by giving up everything that is His.

context.literary:
Chapter 46 reads as the working out of two rules laid down earlier. The first is the rule of the east gate in 44:1 to 3, now qualified: the inner east gate stays shut on the six working days and opens on Sabbaths and New Moons, and for a freewill offering. The second is the prince's duty in 45:17 to supply the offerings, now told as a scene of him actually standing and bowing. The movement is from the gate to the offerings to the daily lamb, then to land, then to kitchens, and the order is deliberate: access, sacrifice, justice and food.

Verses 1 to 15 are framed by the gate. The unit opens with the gate shut and opened, and verses 12 to 15 return to it with the freewill offering and the gate closed again after he goes out. Inside that frame the numbers of animals sit in a tight sequence for Sabbath, New Moon and festival. The refrain 'as much as he is able' in 46:5 and 46:7, for the grain with the lambs, contrasts with the exact amounts for the ram and bull and gives a glimpse of generosity inside the rule.

Verses 16 to 18 break the pattern of sacrifice with a short law about the prince's estate, which is a clear echo of 45:8 to 9. Verses 19 to 24 return to the building, led by the guide, and finish the long section on the house with an unexpected, domestic note: kitchens in the four corners of the outer court. The last words before the river of chapter 47 are about ovens and boiled meat, a reminder that the vision cares about the ordinary meals of ordinary worshippers.
context.historical:
The offerings here differ from those of the Torah in ways that readers have long noticed. Numbers 28:9 to 10 prescribes two lambs on the Sabbath, while Ezekiel 46:4 gives six lambs and a ram. The New Moon in Numbers 28:11 has two bulls, a ram and seven lambs, against one bull, six lambs and a ram in Ezekiel 46:6. The daily offering in Numbers 28:3 to 4 has a lamb in the morning and another at twilight, whereas Ezekiel 46:13 to 15 names only the morning lamb. Ancient and modern readers have taken this as one more sign that the vision is a new, theological ordering and not a copy of the Mosaic code.

The Sabbath and the New Moon were the two regular festivals of Israel's weekly and monthly rhythm, and the prophets had given them a place in worship, Isaiah 66:23. Amos 8:5 shows merchants impatient for both to end so they could return to cheating, which makes this chapter's closing law about land more than an afterthought.

The prince's land law belongs to a world in which kings seized property. Ahab's seizure of Naboth's vineyard, 1 Kings 21, was within living memory of Israel's collective story, and Naboth's reply that the LORD forbade him to give up 'the inheritance of my fathers', 1 Kings 21:3, shows what land meant. Ezekiel had already charged the people's rulers with oppression, 22:29, and the exiles knew what a ruler's overreach looked like.
context.canonical:
The Sabbath and New Moon pair is carried into the prophets' vision of the age to come: 'From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me,' Isaiah 66:23. Ezekiel's gate that opens on those two days and the crowd that bows at it are an earlier version of that picture. The constant morning lamb picks up the daily offering of Exodus 29:38 to 42 and Numbers 28:3 to 8, and John the Baptist's cry, 'Behold, the Lamb of God', John 1:29, draws on this long habit of offering a lamb each day.

The warning about land belongs to the Torah's land theology. The land is the LORD's, Leviticus 25:23, and a person's holding passes to the family and returns in the year of release, Leviticus 25:10. Ezekiel 46:17 uses the same term for freedom, 'the year of freedom', that the Jubilee uses. Isaiah 61:1 then proclaims liberty to captives, and Jesus opens that scroll in Nazareth and declares it fulfilled, Luke 4:18 to 21.

The kitchens echo Zechariah 14:20 to 21, where every pot in Jerusalem is holy. The humble ruler who goes in with the people, and not before them, is carried forward in Jesus, who is 'gentle and humble in heart', Matthew 11:29, and who 'did not come to be served but to serve', Mark 10:45.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel meant the exiles to see that the highest human office in the new age is under the same worship as everyone else. The prince does not enter by the LORD's own gate, he does not offer with his own hands, he bows at the threshold and goes out the way he came, 46:2 and 46:8. Kings in Israel's past had acted as if the Temple were an extension of the palace, and the vision removes that possibility.

The flow of people in verses 9 and 10 carries a second intention. Entering at one gate and leaving at the opposite one keeps the crowd moving, but it also tells every worshipper that no one leaves the way he came. Worship is meant to change the one who comes.

The land law in 46:16 to 18 has a pastoral edge. The people who had lost their homes in the exile are told the next ruler will protect every family's field. The prophet wants a hearer to leave with a picture of a government that guards the weak, and with the hope that the same God who instructs the prince about the gate also instructs him about the poor man's plot.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter prescribes inside a vision, and it does not report events that happened. It also differs on quantities from the Torah, so it cannot be a pattern for Israel in the first Temple, nor can it simply be applied to the church. Christians do not bring a morning lamb or time a gate to the Sabbath and New Moon, since Colossians 2:16 to 17 calls such observances a shadow whose substance is Christ.

The principles do carry across. Rulers are accountable to the same God as those they rule. Public worship should have a rhythm, and the day of rest and the monthly rhythm shape a people. Property of the poor should not be taken by the powerful, and leaders should provide for their own households without displacing others, as 46:18 says. The note that worshippers leave by a different gate is a fitting image of the Christian hope that those who meet God are changed, 2 Corinthians 3:18.

debates.question: Why does the prince offer through the priests when David and Solomon offered themselves?

views.label: A deliberate tightening of priestly boundaries
views.case: David and Solomon are shown offering sacrifices, 2 Samuel 6:17 and 1 Kings 8:62 to 63, and Uzziah was struck when he tried to burn incense, 2 Chronicles 26:16 to 21. The vision, on this reading, settles the matter once for all by having the priests sacrifice his offerings while he stands at the post, 46:2.

views.label: Consistent with the Law all along
views.case: Others point out that Leviticus gives the sacrificing role to the priests and that the king's presence at the altar in the histories is as sponsor and leader of the people. The prince in Ezekiel is still the one who provides and presents the offering; the priests carry out the slaughter.

debates.bearing: Either way, the vision refuses to let the ruler cross into the priest's work, and the New Testament shows the only One who holds both offices without sin, Hebrews 7:1 to 3 and 7:26.

debates.question: What are the differences in the number of animals about?

views.label: A new, theological arrangement
views.case: The numbers follow a pattern of sixes and sevens and do not match Numbers 28 to 29. On this reading the vision is a fresh picture of a restored worship, ordered under a new covenant of the heart, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27, and should not be harmonised.

views.label: Textual or scribal explanations
views.case: Some try to harmonise by supposing that the offerings of Ezekiel are additional to the regular ones, or that ancient numbers have been altered in copying. These proposals are possible, but the text gives no sign of either.

debates.bearing: The difference warns against reading the chapter as a straight copy of the Law. Its message lies in the order and humility of worship, not in matching the arithmetic.

study.originalLanguages:
The central verb of 46:2 and 46:3 is hishtachavah, 'to bow down', from the root shachah. It is the posture of worship and homage, used of Abraham before the three visitors, Genesis 18:2, and of the nations before the LORD in Psalm 96:9. The prince and the people use the same verb, and the same threshold, so that king and commoner share one word and one place. The threshold itself, miftan, is the very word used for the temple threshold from which the river springs in 47:1, so the place where the prince bows is the place from which life will flow.

The prince goes in 'by way of the portico', derekh ulam, and goes out the same way, verses 2 and 8. The ulam is the vestibule, the covered porch of the gatehouse, and the repetition makes the same point as the Hebrew word order: he comes in as he went out, with no road of his own.

The 'freewill offering' in verse 12 is nedavah, from the verb nadav, 'to be willing, to give freely'. It is the offering a person brings out of generosity, not out of obligation, as in Exodus 35:29, where the people brought a nedavah for the tabernacle. The gate is opened even for such a spontaneous gift, which is a remarkable detail: the structure bends to welcome the free heart. The word shelamim, 'peace offerings', in verses 2 and 12, comes from the root shalem, 'whole, complete', and describes the fellowship meal in which the worshipper eats before God.

The morning lamb is called olat tamid, 'a regular burnt offering', in verse 15, and the grain portion is a 'permanent statute', chuqqat olam, in verse 14. The word tamid means continual, unbroken. The morning lamb sets the tone of the day before anything else is done, and without it the temple would not be in daily order.

In verse 17 the servant who receives the prince's gift keeps it only 'until the year of freedom', shenat hadderor. The word deror, 'liberty', is the word of Leviticus 25:10 for the Jubilee and of Isaiah 61:1 for the freedom the anointed one proclaims. Finally the verb bashal, 'to boil', in verse 20 is the word for cooking the sacrificial portions, and the building called the house of the cooks in verse 24 gives the worshipper a place to eat what has been offered.

typology.type: The prince bowing at the threshold with his people, 46:2 and 46:10
typology.fulfillment: The ruler enters when the people enter and leaves when they leave. The picture is of a king who is not above those he leads. Jesus is the Davidic prince who stands among His people, 'I am among you as one who serves', Luke 22:27, and who, though in the form of God, 'emptied Himself', Philippians 2:6 to 8. The correspondence is the humility of the ruler; the escalation is that Christ does not only join the worship but is the Mediator, so that the worshippers come through Him, Hebrews 4:14 to 16. The type falls short because the prince still needs priests to offer for him.

A lamb without blemish is offered every morning, a constant, unbroken offering. John the Baptist points at Jesus and says 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!', John 1:29, and Peter says believers were redeemed by 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:19. Where the daily lamb had to be repeated, Christ 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins', Hebrews 10:12. The daily offering is a shadow that points to the finished work.

typology.type: The year of freedom and the return of the gift, 46:17
typology.fulfillment: A gift to a servant returns to the prince in the year of release, which keeps property in the family and limits how far a gift can reshape the order of the land. Jesus opens Isaiah 61:1 in Nazareth and says 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing', Luke 4:21. The correspondence is liberty proclaimed to those who are bound; the escalation is that Christ proclaims freedom from sin and death, John 8:36, and the year of the Lord's favor has begun, though its full cancellation of debts is still to come.

typology.type: The kitchens at the corners of the court, 46:21 to 24
typology.fulfillment: Ordinary worshippers eat the sacrifices they bring in a place that is kept apart from the holy rooms. The picture points to the Lord's table, where believers eat in the presence of God, 1 Corinthians 10:16 to 17, and to the feast of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The type is only a shadow, because in Ezekiel holiness has to be fenced from the people, whereas in Christ the holy comes near to the people and the table is open to all who are His.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ through the figure of a ruler who is placed under the worship he leads. The prince enters at the same gate as the people and leaves with them, he bows at the threshold, and the priests sacrifice for him, 46:2 and 46:10. Seen alone, the prince is only a man, and 45:22 has already shown he needs a sin offering for himself. But in the light of Ezekiel 34:24 and 37:25, where God promises 'My servant David will be a prince among them', the prince is a signpost to the Son of David who is both ruler and servant. Jesus 'did not come to be served but to serve', Mark 10:45, and washed His disciples' feet, John 13:14. Philippians 2:6 to 8 describes the descent exactly: the One who was in the form of God took the form of a servant and became obedient to death.

The daily lamb is the second line. The morning offering of 46:13 to 15, unblemished and unbroken, is a standing reminder that sin needs covering every day. John the Baptist names Jesus as the lamb, John 1:29, and Hebrews 10:11 to 14 says the priest stands 'day after day' offering the same sacrifices which can never take away sins, but Christ 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins' and sat down. The tamid is fulfilled not by being repeated but by being completed.

The prince's duty not to take the people's land, 46:18, carries a third strand. The messianic King in Psalm 72 delivers the needy and crushes the oppressor, and Jesus identifies His mission with the Jubilee, Luke 4:18 to 19. The care for the dispossessed in this chapter points to the Messiah who gives the meek the inheritance, Matthew 5:5.

The gate that opens for the freewill offering carries a last strand: 'the one who comes to Me I will never drive away', John 6:37. The East gate opens to the willing heart. A caution is needed. The corner kitchens, the exact oven placements and the number of lambs should not be treated as hidden portraits of Christ. What the New Testament takes up is the shape of a humble king, a constant lamb, a gift that frees and a table where common worshippers eat in the presence of God.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who is careful about how He is approached, and a God who is generous about who may approach. The gate opens on Sabbath and New Moon, and also for a freewill offering, 46:1 and 46:12, so His rules for worship are not stingy. The same house that keeps its east gate shut on working days opens it to a willing heart on any day.

He is a God who wants worship to move. People enter by one gate and leave by another, 46:9, and nobody goes back the way he came. That small rule has a theology in it. An encounter with the living God is not a place to return to unchanged. The visitor is sent out on a new road.

He is a God of justice who guards the weak against the strong. The prince is told he may not 'take any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property', 46:18, and the reason is spelled out: 'so that none of My people will be displaced from his property'. The phrase 'My people' matters. The land belongs to the LORD, Leviticus 25:23, and God does not let a ruler treat His people's holdings as his own. He is the defender of the poor, as in Psalm 68:5 and Proverbs 22:22 to 23.

He is a God who cares for the ordinary meal. The last scene of the temple's plan is not a throne room or an altar but a kitchen. The priests cook the people's sacrifices in a place designed so that holiness does not harm the laity, 46:20, and the people eat from what they brought, 46:24. The God of Sinai who sets a boundary around the mountain also arranges for the worshipper to be fed.

He is a God of steadiness. The daily lamb is a 'permanent statute', 46:14, and His worship has a rhythm of day, week and month that shapes the life of His people. For worship, the chapter calls us to come with a willing heart, to expect that He will send us out changed, to treat our leaders as fellow worshippers and not rivals, and to remember that He feeds His people in His own house.

crossReferences.note: The east gate shut because the LORD entered by it, with the prince permitted only to eat in its portico. Chapter 46 qualifies the rule: on Sabbaths, New Moons and freewill offerings the inner gate opens, but the prince still enters by the portico and leaves the same way.

The Sabbath offering in the Torah is two lambs with a grain offering. Ezekiel 46:4 raises it to six lambs and a ram, a difference that tells the reader the vision is a new ordering and not a restatement.

The daily offering of a lamb in the morning and another at twilight is the origin of the 'regular burnt offering'. Ezekiel 46:13 to 15 keeps the morning lamb and calls it a permanent statute, so the day still begins with a sacrifice.

The Jubilee proclaims liberty and returns each person to his property. The 'year of freedom' in Ezekiel 46:17 uses the same word for liberty, so the prince's gift to a servant is bound by the same rhythm of release that protects every family's land.

Elijah's charge against Ahab asks 'Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?' This is the abuse Ezekiel 46:18 forbids to the prince, and it shows that the vision is built from the memory of what happened under kings.

All humankind will come to worship 'from one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another.' Ezekiel 46:1 to 3 gives the same two days a specific place at the east gate, so the nations' worship in Isaiah and Israel's in Ezekiel share one rhythm.

Every cooking pot in Jerusalem becomes holy to the LORD, and those who sacrifice take pots and boil in them. Ezekiel 46:20 to 24 provides the kitchens where the offering is cooked, and Zechariah pictures the day when holiness has spread so far that ordinary vessels share it.

Christ, in the form of God, took the form of a servant and was obedient to death. The prince of Ezekiel 46 who stands with his people and bows at the threshold is a faint picture of the greater Prince who humbled Himself and shares our worship.

John calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.' The daily morning lamb of Ezekiel 46:13 to 15 is the pattern behind that title, and the permanent lamb of the vision is replaced by a Lamb who finishes the work.

Jesus reads Isaiah 61, proclaiming liberty to captives and the year of the Lord's favor, which uses the same word for freedom as Ezekiel 46:17. His announcement carries the Jubilee beyond a return of land to the release of people.

study.oneStory:
Before this chapter the Bible has told of a God who dwelt with Adam in a garden, walked among Israel in the tabernacle and then left a Temple that His people had defiled. The question hanging over the exile is whether God can ever again live with a people who keep failing Him, and whether anyone who rules them can be trusted. The vision of 40 to 48 answers with a rebuilt house and a restored people, and chapter 46 is where that answer turns into a pattern of ordinary life: how a king worships, how a crowd moves, what is offered each morning, who owns the land and how a family eats.

What the chapter answers from before is the history of kings. Saul, David, Solomon and the kings of Israel and Judah all stand in the story as rulers who either led the people to the LORD or took from them. Ahab's seizure of Naboth's vineyard is the clearest case, 1 Kings 21. Ezekiel's prince is a correction written into the future: a ruler who is bound by the Law and stands beside his people.

What the chapter sets up is the Messiah. The prince who holds a lowly place at the threshold, the lamb offered every morning, the year of freedom and the table of the people all find their fulfilment in Jesus, who is King, Priest and Lamb in one person, John 1:29, Hebrews 4:14 and Luke 4:18 to 21. The people who once came to a gate now 'draw near with a sincere heart', Hebrews 10:22, and the royal priesthood is the whole church, 1 Peter 2:9.

The story ends in a city where the gates are never shut and where no one needs a temple, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple', Revelation 21:22 to 25. The east gate that opened only for Sabbath and New Moon, and the lamb offered each morning, give way to a city with no night and a Lamb who is its lamp, Revelation 21:23, and the nations who once bowed at a threshold bring their glory in, Revelation 21:26.

quiz.q: How does the prince enter and leave the inner east gate on the Sabbath?

options.text: He enters through the portico of the gateway and stands by the gatepost, then departs the same way
options.note: 46:2 and 46:8 describe exactly this pattern of entry and exit.

options.text: He enters through the gate reserved only for the LORD in chapter 44
options.note: That gate remains permanently shut to everyone, including the prince, per 44:2.

options.text: He is carried in by the priests as part of the ceremony
options.note: The text describes him entering and standing on his own, not being carried.

options.text: He offers the sacrifice himself at the altar before departing
options.note: The priests sacrifice on his behalf, 46:2; the prince does not personally minister at the altar.

quiz.q: What rule governs the people's movement through the gates during the appointed feasts?

options.text: Whoever enters by one gate must leave by the opposite gate, not returning the way they came
options.note: 46:9 states this rule precisely, north to south and south to north.

options.text: Everyone must enter and exit by the east gate only
options.note: The east gate belongs to the LORD and the prince; the people use the north and south gates.

options.text: Men and women use separate, permanently assigned gates
options.note: The distinction given is about entry versus exit direction, not gender-assigned gates.

options.text: The order of entry depends on tribal rank
options.note: No tribal ranking of gate use is given; the rule is about direction of travel, not tribe.

quiz.q: What does 46:18 explicitly forbid the prince from doing?

options.text: Taking any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property
options.note: 46:18 states this prohibition directly, protecting ordinary Israelites' land.

options.text: Offering freewill offerings on behalf of the people
options.note: Freewill offerings by the prince are described positively in 46:12, not forbidden.

options.text: Giving any gift to his own sons
options.note: 46:16 explicitly permits and protects such gifts as a lasting inheritance for his sons.

options.text: Entering the temple on ordinary working days
options.note: The gate is simply shut on working days for everyone, not a specific prohibition aimed at the prince alone.

quiz.q: Why are the sin offering and grain offering boiled and baked in a separate chamber rather than the outer court?

options.text: So that the priests do not transmit holiness to the people through contact with these offerings in the outer court
options.note: 46:20 gives this exact reason for the guarded location.

options.text: Because the outer court had no ovens or cooking facilities at all
options.note: The outer court's corners in fact contain their own kitchens, 46:21-24, for different sacrifices.

options.text: Because only Levites, and no priests, were permitted to cook
options.note: The text specifically assigns this cooking to the priests, not Levites.

options.text: To keep the meat from spoiling in the open air
options.note: The stated concern is transmitting holiness to the people, not food preservation.

quiz.q: How does Philippians 2 illuminate the prince's humble pattern of worship in this chapter?

options.text: Christ, though equal with God, did not grasp that equality but emptied Himself and humbled Himself as a servant, the pattern the prince's non-grasping worship anticipates
options.note: Philippians 2:6-8 describes this humility, which the prince's careful, ordinary access pictures in shadow.

options.text: Christ claimed the same exclusive entrance reserved for the LORD alone, unlike the prince
options.note: This misreads Philippians 2, which stresses Christ's humility and self-emptying, not a grasping for exclusive access.

options.text: Christ abolished the need for any ordered access to God whatsoever
options.note: Hebrews, not Philippians 2, addresses access to God, and even there Christ opens a way rather than abolishing order.

options.text: Christ became a priest exactly like the sons of Zadok, with no distinction
options.note: Hebrews 7 stresses Christ's priesthood is of a different, greater order than Zadok's line, not identical to it.

questions: The prince worships exactly as the people do, entering and leaving by the same gate. Where might God be calling you to set aside any assumed privilege and worship simply as one among His people?

The rule to exit by the opposite gate meant no one could linger where they entered, keeping worship moving and orderly. Is there a habit in your own worship life that has grown careless or complacent that this picture of intentional order might correct?

God explicitly protects ordinary people's inheritance from a ruler's seizure. Where do you see power being used to take rather than to give in your own sphere, and how might you use whatever influence you have differently?
The sin offering had to be handled carefully so its holiness would not spread carelessly. How does this shape your understanding of reverence in worship, even under the freedom Christ has won for us?

Christ, though equal with God, did not grasp at that equality but emptied Himself. Where in your life is God inviting you to imitate that kind of humility rather than grasping for status or recognition?

translationNotes.note: 'Bow in worship at the threshold' pictures prostration, a physical posture of submission that the prince shares with the ordinary people named in 46:3, underlining that his worship is of the same kind as theirs.
'To moisten the fine flour' describes mixing oil into the grain offering.

'The year of freedom' almost certainly refers to the jubilee year of Leviticus 25, when property given away reverts to its original owner, here applied specifically to protect the prince's sons from losing their permanent inheritance.
